title: The Rule-Breaker's Biggest Win

beats.text: The father of value investing made his biggest profit breaking his own rule.
It's New York, nineteen forty-eight. You work for Benjamin Graham.
His rule: about five percent, tops, in any one stock.
He's so careful, he'd diversify his lunch.
Then a small car insurer comes up for sale.
It sells by mail to government workers. No agents.
Graham buys half of it for seven hundred twelve thousand dollars.
About a fifth of the fund, in one stock.
Why would Wall Street's most careful man do that?
You see, it's a lemonade stand with no middleman. Cheaper cups, longer line.
Cheaper policies, more drivers, and the company kept growing.
By nineteen seventy-two, that stake was worth four hundred million dollars.
Graham wrote that one decision beat all his others, over twenty years, combined.
One lucky break, or one supremely shrewd decision. Can we tell them apart?

facts.claim: In 1948 Benjamin Graham's Graham-Newman Corp. bought half (50%) of GEICO for $712,000
Graham-Newman normally diversified widely, seldom more than about 5% in one holding; the GEICO stake was roughly 20% (about one fifth) of the fund
GEICO, founded 1936 by Leo and Lillian Goodwin, sold auto insurance directly by mail to government employees, without agents; based in Washington, D.C. from 1937
The Graham-Newman GEICO position was worth about $400 million by 1972 (a more than 200-fold gain)

Graham's postscript to The Intelligent Investor: profits from this single decision far exceeded the sum of all others realized through 20 years; 'one lucky break, or one supremely shrewd decision - can we tell them apart?'
Graham is called the father of value investing; he died in 1976 (deceased)

caption:
1948: Benjamin Graham, who rarely put more than about 5% into one stock, bought half of a small mail-order car insurer for $712,000. About a fifth of his fund.
By 1972 it was worth some $400 million. His own verdict: lucky, or shrewd? Can we tell them apart?
